items.title: Overview
items.text:
This site presents the requirements for the written part of the Science Olympian 2027 competitions for Divisions B and C.

The requirements for Div. B are generally the same as Div. C, but differences in Part I the written test are described B_vs_C.md.

Additional requirements for Div. B and Div. C in the State and National competitions are shown Local_vs_State.

items.title: 1. Joseph Black (1728-1799) (Scottish) (University of Glasgow)
items.text:
Known for:

  • 1750: invention of the analytical balance, which was far more accurate than other balances at that time.
  • 1754: the discovery of carbon dioxide. Black called it "fixed air" bc it was fixed inside solids. He discovered it by heating limestone.
  • 1755: the discovery of Magnesium. Black distinguished between magnesia (now called magnesium oxide) and lime (now called calcium oxide).
  • 1760: discovery of specific heat
  • 1761: discovery of latent heat

items.title: James Prescott Joule

Before Joule's work, it was widely recognized tht mechanical work could be turned into heat.

Joule was the first to perform a careful experiment which determined the mechanical equivalent of heat, using a paddle wheel apparatus.

items.title: Sensible vs. Latent Heat
items.text:
Sensible heat changes an object's temperature and can be measured with a standard thermometer.

Latent heat changes a substance's physical state (like turning liquid water into steam) without altering its temperature.

items.title: Sensible Heat
items.text:
• Definition: Energy that causes a direct rise or fall in temperature.

  • Measurement: Read easily with a thermometer.

  • State of matter: No phase change occurs; the substance stays solid, liquid, or gas.

  • Examples: Warm air blowing from a furnace, a hot cup of coffee cooling down, or sunshine warming a room.

items.title: Latent Heat
items.text:
• Definition: "Hidden" energy stored or released during a phase change.

  • Measurement: Cannot be measured using a standard thermometer because the temperature doesn't change.

  • State of matter: Changes phase, such as solid to liquid or liquid to gas.

  • Examples: Ice melting into water at 32F, water boiling into steam at 212F, or an air conditioner condensing humidity out of the air.

items.title: What is a thermodynamic system?
items.text:
A thermodynamic system is a specific, defined region of the universe—-like a container of gas, an engine, or a living cell-—chosen for scientific study.

A thermodynamic system is separated from everything else (its surroundings) by a boundary. The boundary may be physical (such as a box or enclosed room), or hypothetical (such as a specified region of space).

So the core components of a thermodynamic system are:

  1. System: the exact matter or region in space being analyzed.

  2. Boundary: the real or imaginary wall that separates the system from what is outside it.

  3. Surroundings: everything in the universe outside the system's boundary.

Thermodynamic systems differ in how they interact with their surrundings:

  • Open System: Exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings (e.g., a boiling pot of water without a lid).

    Examples: a boiling pot of water without a lid

  • Closed System: Exchanges energy but not matter (e.g., a sealed, rigid metal container filled with hot gas).

    Examples: a sealed, rigid metal container filled with hot gas

  • Isolated System: Exchanges neither matter nor energy (e.g., a perfect, thermally insulated thermos).

    Examples: a perfect, thermally insulated thermos

items.title: Properties of a Thermodynamic System
items.text: See this page on intensive and extensive properties

items.title: Intensive properties
items.text:
An intensive property of a thermodynamic system does not depend on the system's size or the amount of matter present.

Some characteristics of intensive properties are:

  • Independent of size: changing the sample mass does not change the value.

  • Ratio of extensive values: Dividing one extensive property by another extensive property (like mass or volume) creates an intensive property.

  • Can vary locally: : While uniform in equilibrium, intensive properties like pressure or temperature can vary from point to point within a non-equilibrium system.

Common examples include:

  • Temperature, e.g. hot or cold

  • Pressure, i.e., Force per unit area

  • Density, i.e., mass divided by volume

  • Boiling and Melting Points: temperature where phase changes happen.

  • Specific properties: any extensive property divided by mass, e.g. specific volume or specific enthalpy.

items.title: Heat Trasnfer
items.text:
Heat transfer moves thermal energy from a warmer area to a cooler area. The three main types are conduction, convection, and radiation.

Other, novel modes of heat conduction carry out energy transport in advanced electronics, nanomaterials, and ultrafast laser interactions. These modes are not listed here (yet).

items.title: Conduction
items.text:
How it works: Heat moves through direct physical contact between objects or materials. Atoms or molecules bump into each other and pass along their energy without the material itself moving.

Best medium: Solids (metals like copper and iron are great conductors).

Example: A metal spoon getting hot when left in a bowl of hot soup.

items.title: Convection
items.text:
How it works: Heat moves through the actual movement of fluids, which means liquids and gases. Warm fluid gets less dense and rises, while cooler fluid sinks to take its place, creating a circular motion called a convection current.

Best medium: Liquids and gases.

Example: Boiling water rolling in a pot, where hot water at the bottom rises to the top.

items.title: Radiation
items.text:
How it works: Heat moves through empty space via invisible electromagnetic waves (like infrared rays). It does not need any matter, air, or physical contact to travel.

Best medium: Vacuum or empty space.

Example: The Sun warming the Earth from millions of miles away across space.

items.title: Advection
items.text:
How it works: The transfer of heat from one location to another through the bulk physical motion of a fluid. While similar to convection, it specifically refers to horizontal or forced movement. Example:

Example: Warm ocean currents, such as the Gulf Stream, carrying heat across the Atlantic.

items.title: Micro- and Nano-scale conduction
items.text:
Modern thermal engineering recognizes novel forms of heat conduction that apply to energy transport in advanced electronics, nano materials, and ultrafast laserinteractions.

(These topics may not be covered by either the B or C Science Olympiad tests, but for the curious, see this page for a short overview of these conduction methods.)

items.title: Heat Transport at Small Scales
items.text: While classical physics recognizes conduction, convection, and radiation, modern microscale and nanoscale thermal engineering explores novel, non-Fourier, and quantum-level mechanisms of heat transfer. These mechanisms dictate energy transport in advanced electronics, nanomaterials, and ultrafast laser interactions.

items.title: Ballistic and Non-Fourier Conduction
items.text:
At micro and nano dimensions, heat carriers do not diffuse randomly as described by standard Fourier laws; instead, they travel like waves or projectiles.

  • Ballistic Phonon Transport: Heat moves through a crystal lattice via quantized vibrations (phonons) without undergoing any scattering events over short distances, bypassing traditional thermal resistance.

  • Second Sound: A quantum hydrodynamic phenomenon in super-cold or highly conductive materials where thermal energy propagates through a crystal as an actual wavelike second-sound pulse rather than slow diffusion.

items.title: Near-Field and Polaritonic Radiation
items.text:
Standard thermal radiation is limited by blackbody laws and far-field assumptions, but novel geometries alter this fundamentally.

  • Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer: When objects are separated by distances smaller than the dominant thermal wavelength (nanometers apart), electromagnetic tunneling occurs, allowing heat radiation exchange to exceed standard blackbody limits by orders of magnitude.

  • Surface Polariton Coupling: Thermal energy couples with electromagnetic surface waves (plasmon-polaritons or phonon-polaritons) at material interfaces, channeling radiant energy across boundaries with high efficiency

items.title: Ultrafast and Interfacial Energy Transduction
items.text:
• Electron-Phonon Nonequilibrium: In metals heated by ultrafast lasers, electrons reach extreme temperatures while the atomic lattice remains cold, transferring energy through unique electron-phonon coupling and non-equilibrium scattering mechanics.

  • Transient Granular Vortices: Microscopic fluid-like or granular vortex motions generated in sheared materials (such as tectonic fault lines) can yield effective thermal diffusivities vastly higher than static conduction
